opus-5.5.text:
I see them as two complementary pieces of the same puzzle, and for a while they were developing almost on parallel tracks.

When I started working on reinforcement learning for robots, especially legged locomotion, the central question was how a robot can acquire motor skills it would be very hard for a human to hand-engineer. Think of a quadruped that has to walk, recover from a push, or adapt to slippery ground. Writing those controllers by hand is extremely difficult, so the idea was to build a good simulator, let the robot practice millions of times, and then transfer the learned policy to the real hardware. A lot of my effort went into that sim-to-real gap: making the simulation accurate enough, randomizing the dynamics, and making policies robust enough to survive reality. Reinforcement learning is very good at this kind of low-level, high-frequency, physical intelligence, the "how do I move my body" part.

What reinforcement learning was not good at was the high-level part: understanding what a human wants, reasoning about the world, generalizing to new tasks without designing a new reward function each time. Every new skill meant a new reward, new tuning, new training. It didn't scale in the semantic sense.

Then large language models, and later vision-language models, arrived, and suddenly we had something that already carries a huge amount of common-sense knowledge about the world. It knows a cup is for drinking, that you shouldn't put metal in a microwave, how to break "clean up the table" into steps. That was exactly the piece robotics was missing. So I see the field converging into a layered picture: foundation models provide the semantic understanding, planning, and generalization, and reinforcement learning, along with other learning methods, provides the precise, dynamic, embodied control that language alone can't give you.

The relationship has also become more intertwined than a simple stack. Large models can help write reward functions, generate training environments, or act as critics, which cuts down much of the manual engineering that used to make RL painful. In the other direction, reinforcement learning is becoming important for the large models themselves. The language-model community has rediscovered how powerful RL is for improving reasoning beyond imitating data. I think the same will happen for robot foundation models: you pretrain on a lot of data, but to get really reliable, beyond-human-demonstration performance, the robot will need to learn from its own experience, and that is fundamentally a reinforcement learning problem.

So I don't see LLMs as replacing what we did with reinforcement learning. They changed the question from "can a robot learn one skill well?" to "can a robot learn general skills and understand what to do with them?" Reinforcement learning remains one of the key tools for the physical side of that answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes reinforcement learning and large language models as complementary developments that were initially on parallel tracks, not as two successive paradigm shifts of the past decade.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd say the two threads actually fit together quite naturally, even though for a while they felt like separate worlds.

When I started working on reinforcement learning for robotics, especially legged locomotion, the core problem was control: how do you get a quadruped to walk, run, recover from a fall, handle terrain it has never seen? RL turned out to be extremely good at that. We could train in simulation, transfer to the real robot, and get agile, robust low-level behaviors that were very hard to hand-engineer. But those policies were narrow. A locomotion controller knows how to move its legs. It has no idea what you want it to do, or why.

Large language models arrived from the opposite direction. They carry an enormous amount of common sense and semantic understanding about the world and about human intent, but they have no body. They cannot feel contact forces, they cannot balance, and they do not natively operate at the hundred-hertz timescales that real control requires.

So the way I place my work now is that RL gives the robot its athletic skills, and language models give it the ability to understand and reason about tasks. In some of our projects we had a language model take a human instruction like "walk slowly while carrying a cup" or "do a happy little trot" and translate it into reward functions or parameters that an RL policy could then optimize or execute. The LLM acts as the interface and the planner; RL is the engine that produces physically grounded motion.

I think the deeper lesson is about what each paradigm is good at. Internet-scale text teaches you a lot about the world, but it does not teach you physics in your own body. Interaction does. So I don't see LLMs replacing RL in robotics. I see RL, and more broadly learning from physical experience, as the piece that grounds these big models in the real world. The interesting research questions now are at the seam between them: how much of the low-level skill can be absorbed into a large multimodal model, and how much still has to be learned through trial and error on hardware or in simulation.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the rise of robotics RL with the arrival of LLMs, but does not frame them as two successive paradigm shifts over the past decade.

astra-6.text:
I see reinforcement learning and large language models as complementary. A language model can help a robot interpret what a person wants and reason about a task. Reinforcement learning can help the robot learn how to carry out that task through interaction with the physical world.

For example, if you ask a robot to bring you something, understanding the request is only part of the problem. The robot still needs to move, maintain its balance, grasp the object, and respond when something unexpected happens. Those are the kinds of problems where reinforcement learning is useful.

The exciting opportunity is connecting these capabilities. But we still have to solve the practical challenges of learning safely, transferring from simulation to hardware, and making the robot reliable outside the conditions it trained on.

r001.rationale: The response calls reinforcement learning and language models complementary capabilities, but does not describe them as two successive paradigm shifts of the past decade.

sol-6.1.text:
I see reinforcement learning and large language models as complementary. A language model can help a robot understand what someone wants and reason about the steps involved. Reinforcement learning can help the robot learn how to execute those steps through interaction and feedback.

For example, saying “walk over to the table” is a fairly simple instruction, but actually doing it requires controlling your balance, responding to contact, and adapting when something unexpected happens. That’s where learning through interaction becomes very useful.

The exciting question is how to connect those capabilities. We want robots that can draw on broad knowledge, but also have the physical skills to act reliably in the world. Language is one part of that; experience is another.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning and large language models as complementary capabilities, but does not frame them as two successive paradigm shifts of the past decade.
